hook: This one is funnier than its object class suggests. A small, warm green ball oozes a harmless and even useful slime, and there is exactly one thing it must never touch. Read it with an ear for repetition, because the joke builds sentence by sentence.
whyItMatters: It shows how comedy can be carried entirely by the clinical Foundation voice. Instead of breaking format for a gag, it keeps every line deadpan and lets one restriction recur until it becomes absurd. It also treats an anomaly as a handy resource, with salad dressing and fuel savings sitting right next to grim warnings.
thingsToNotice:
Count how often the phrase about dead bodies is bolted onto the end of an otherwise cheerful sentence: the slime is edible, boosts gasoline mileage by 150%, refines into a Foundation-approved lubricant that must never be used on corpses, and staff are polygraph-screened for suicidal, homicidal or necrophiliac urges. The repetition works as a running gag while making you more and more curious about what actually happens on contact.

The article never tells you. The one sentence that would explain it is cut off by an O5 notice threatening execution or demotion to D-class for anyone who researches the subject, the retrieval report and incident appendices it points to are not included, and the final addendum downgrades it from Keter to Safe with the same caveat attached once more.
